newsitem.title: UK: UK's Manchester Airport told to reduce charges.
newsitem.headline: UK's Manchester Airport told to reduce charges.

text.p: Britain's locally run Manchester Airport, recently voted as one of the world's top two airports, will be asked to reduce its airport charges over the next five years by UK's Civil Aviation Authority, the regulatory body said on Tuesday.

The CAA said it would implement the recommendations made by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC), which said its income per passenger from airport charges should fall by RPI-6.6 in 1998/99 and RPI-5 in each of the following four years implying a dip of 6.6 or five percentage points less than the rate of inflation.
CAA said the recommendations incorporated the adjustment for the expected loss of net revenue from intra-European duty free sales from July 1999.
Under the UK's 1986 Airports Act, the CAA refers Manchester Airport to the MMC every five years.

The MMC in turn reports to CAA on what the maximum level of airport charges should be at the airport for the next five years and whether over the last five years the airport has acted against the public interest in any way.

CAA said that the proposed formula would bring down Manchester's permitted charges by almost a quarter in real terms between 1997/98 and 2002/03 and bring them closer to those at Gatwick Airport, UK's second largest after London Heathrow.
"The CAA believes that the MMC's analysis shows that Manchester Airport would still be able to pursue its current investment plans," it said.
The MMC also accused Manchester Airport of providing inadequate information to airport tenants on the costs and revenues associated with the supply of utilities including gas and electricity.
MMC also said the airport was inadequate in its procedures on capital investment, on structure of airport charges, on the level of other charges and quality of service.
"The CAA is proposing conditions to ensure that Manchester Airport addresses these problems," CAA said.
The International Air Transport Association (IATA) said last April that Singapore's Changi and the Machester Airport had been voted the worlds' top two airports by long-haul airline passengers.
